title: Professional behaviour & social media
blurb: Behaving professionally at work, outside work and online: boundaries with patients, gifts, phone numbers and what you must never post.
question: A grateful patient gives you a £50 gift card and asks for your mobile number 'in case my tooth plays up at the weekend'. That evening a friend tags you in a photo taken in the surgery, posted on Instagram. What are the professional issues, and what should you do?

teach.body: GDC Principle 9 says your personal behaviour must maintain patients' confidence in you and in the dental profession. That covers how you act at work, in your private life and online. The GDC can investigate conduct outside work, such as dishonesty, violence, drink-driving or offensive posts, because it affects whether the public can trust you. You must tell the GDC if you are subject to criminal proceedings or a regulatory finding. Being a professional is part of who you are, not just a uniform you take off at 5 pm.

rows.label: Advice
values: Book them in to be seen

teach.h: Social media: what the GDC expects
teach.body: Confidentiality applies online exactly as it does in the surgery. Never post anything about a patient without consent. Even 'anonymous' cases can identify someone, and background details such as a screen, a chart, a name on a lab bag or a mirror reflection can give a person away. Privacy settings don't make a post private: screenshots travel. Don't post comments that are discriminatory, abusive or that criticise colleagues or patients. Posting under a nickname doesn't change your responsibility. Follow your practice's social media policy too.

steps.label: Could anyone be identified?
steps.sub: Check faces, screens, notes and the background

steps.label: Would I show it to a patient?
Is it fair to colleagues?
steps.sub: No complaints or gossip about work

teach.caption: If you're tagged in something unprofessional, ask for it to be removed and tell your manager if it involves patients.

teach.body: The GDC says you must refuse gifts, payment or hospitality if accepting could affect, or could appear to affect, your professional judgement. Chocolates for the whole team are usually fine. Cash, vouchers or expensive personal gifts need more thought: follow your practice's gifts policy, which may mean declining or declaring it to the manager. Never let a gift change how a patient is treated or prioritised. Don't give patients your personal phone number. Contact goes through the practice, and out-of-hours problems go to the practice's emergency arrangements or NHS 111.

teach.h: Gifts: from fine to not acceptable

bands.label: Gift tied to a favour, e.g. jumping the queue

teach.caption: The test is not the price tag alone: could it affect, or look as though it affects, your judgement?

teach.text: A surgery photo with 'no patient in it' can still breach confidentiality. A computer screen, a day list, a chart on the wall or a name on a model box can identify someone.

items: Principle 9 covers your behaviour at work, outside work and online.
Never post patient information or surgery images that could identify anyone, even in the background.
Keep boundaries: no personal numbers, no friend requests from patients, no clinical advice by DM.
Refuse gifts that could affect, or appear to affect, your judgement; follow the practice gifts policy.
Tell the GDC about criminal proceedings or regulatory findings.

summary: You can now explain how GDC Principle 9 applies inside and outside work, keep professional boundaries with patients, check a post before sharing it, and decide when a gift can be accepted and when it must be declined or declared.

A.q: A dental nurse posts a photo of the surgery on social media with no patient visible. What is the main risk?
options: The surgery may look untidy to patients
Identifiable details may be in the background
It advertises the practice without the owner's approval
Other nurses may copy the idea and post too
A.why: Screens, charts, day lists or names on lab work can identify patients, breaching confidentiality.

whyNot.2: Advertising isn't the main risk; confidentiality is.
whyNot.3: Copying isn't the issue; the content could identify patients.

A.q: A patient asks for your personal phone number so they can ask questions later. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Give it, as it helps the patient
Give it, but say it's only for real emergencies
Explain contact goes through the practice
Give a colleague's number instead
A.why: Personal numbers blur professional boundaries. Patients should contact the practice, or its out-of-hours arrangements.

whyNot.0: Helpful intent doesn't make it appropriate.
whyNot.1: Emergencies have proper routes, such as the practice's out-of-hours service or NHS 111.
whyNot.3: Sharing a colleague's number breaks their privacy and the same boundary.

A.q: A patient sends you a friend request on your personal social media account. What should you do?
options: Accept, but don't discuss treatment
Accept and restrict what they see
Accept, but only once their course of treatment ends
Decline politely and keep it professional
A.why: Keeping patients off personal accounts maintains professional boundaries and protects confidentiality.

whyNot.0: Being 'friends' still blurs the professional relationship.
whyNot.1: Restrictions don't remove the boundary problem.
whyNot.2: They may well return as a patient; the boundary still matters.

B.q: A grateful patient offers you a gift. What is the main professional consideration?
options: Whether it could affect, or seem to affect, care
Whether it has been gift-wrapped for you
Whether your colleagues were given one too
Whether it is worth less than the £100 limit in total
B.why: The GDC test is whether accepting could affect, or appear to affect, your professional judgement.

whyNot.2: Fairness between staff isn't the professional test.
whyNot.3: There's no fixed GDC price limit; the test is influence.

B.q: Which GDC principle is most directly about your conduct outside work?
options: Principle 7: knowledge and skills
Principle 9: personal behaviour
Principle 3: valid consent
Principle 5: complaints
B.why: Principle 9 requires your personal behaviour to maintain confidence in you and the profession, including outside work.

whyNot.0: Principle 7 concerns scope, training and CPD.

B.q: A patient messages your personal account asking whether their swollen gum needs antibiotics. What should you do?
options: Reply with some general advice about it
Ask them to send a photo so you can assess
Advise contacting the practice to be seen
Ignore the message and say nothing
B.why: Clinical advice must come through proper channels. Direct them to contact the practice so a clinician can assess them.

whyNot.0: Giving clinical advice privately is outside proper boundaries and your scope.
whyNot.1: Assessing a photo is diagnosis, which is outside a nurse's scope.
whyNot.3: Ignoring a possible problem isn't in the patient's interest; signpost them.

C.q: A colleague shares an 'anonymous' story online about a difficult patient, without naming them. Why is this a problem?
options: Only dentists may post about patients
It is too long for social media
The patient may still be identifiable
It wasn't approved by the GDC
C.why: Details such as the date, treatment or behaviour can be enough for the patient or others to recognise them.

whyNot.0: No registrant may share identifiable patient information without consent.
whyNot.3: The GDC doesn't approve posts; confidentiality is the issue.

C.q: A dental nurse receives a police caution for a public order offence. What must she do?
options: Nothing, as it happened outside work
Tell only her employer
Wait until her registration renewal
Inform the GDC
C.why: Registrants must tell the GDC about criminal proceedings, such as cautions or convictions.

whyNot.1: Telling the employer may be required too, but the GDC must be informed.
whyNot.2: She must not delay telling the GDC.

C.q: A patient hands you £20 cash 'for being so kind'. What is the best response?
options: Accept it and say nothing
Decline or declare it, per practice policy
Accept it and buy treats for the whole team
Accept it, as refusing is rude
C.why: Cash gifts can look as though they influence care. Follow the practice gifts policy, which usually means declining politely or declaring it.

whyNot.0: Keeping quiet about a cash gift risks the appearance of influence.
whyNot.2: Sharing it doesn't remove the problem of accepting cash.
whyNot.3: You can decline kindly; politeness doesn't outweigh professional boundaries.

reteach.title: The noticeboard test
reteach.question: Imagine anything you post, say or accept could be pinned on the practice noticeboard for patients and the GDC to see. Would you still do it?

blocks.h: Would you be happy for it to be seen?
blocks.body: Professional behaviour comes down to trust. Patients trust you with their mouths, their health and their private information. Anything that makes them wonder whether they can trust you damages that: a post mocking a patient, a gift that buys a better slot, a personal number that turns a professional relationship into a friendship. Before acting, picture it on the noticeboard. If you'd be uncomfortable, don't do it.

rows.label: Sharing the practice's official oral health post
Selfie in uniform with a screen behind you
Joking about a nervous patient in a group chat

items.label: patient friend requests on personal accounts

explain.body: Your behaviour at work, in private and online must maintain trust in you and the profession. Tell the GDC about criminal proceedings.

test.q: Why can the GDC act on a dental nurse's behaviour outside work?
options: Because it can affect public trust
Because the practice owns her time
Because all nurses are on call
Because the GDC is her employer
test.why: Conduct outside work can affect whether the public can trust a registrant, which is what Principle 9 protects.

whyNot.1: The practice doesn't own her private time.
whyNot.3: The GDC is the regulator, not the employer.

explain.body: Confidentiality applies online. Check backgrounds, don't post about patients, don't criticise colleagues, and don't give clinical advice through personal accounts.

test.q: Which of these posts is most likely to breach patient confidentiality?
options: A practice award photo with only staff in shot
A photo with a day list visible behind you
A post sharing NHS toothbrushing advice for parents
A post about your CPD course
test.why: A visible day list shows patient names, so it identifies patients.

whyNot.0: Staff-only photos with no patient details are generally fine.
whyNot.2: Sharing public health advice doesn't involve patient data.

explain.body: Refuse gifts that could affect, or appear to affect, your judgement; follow the gifts policy. Keep contact through the practice, never your personal number.

bands.label: Cash, or linked to a favour

test.q: A patient offers an expensive bottle of wine if you can 'squeeze them in' next week. What should you do?
options: Accept and book them in
Accept but don't change the booking
Decline, and book them in as normal
Ask for something less expensive
test.why: The gift is tied to a favour, so accepting would affect, or appear to affect, how they are treated. Decline and treat them like anyone else.

whyNot.0: This lets a gift buy priority.
whyNot.1: Accepting still looks like it buys influence.
whyNot.3: The problem is the link to a favour, not the price.
